source.title: Understanding Emergent Misalignment via Feature Superposition Geometry
source.authors: Gouki Minegishi; Hiroki Furuta; Takeshi Kojima; Yusuke Iwasawa; Yutaka Matsuo

record.file_problem: None; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: It applies narrow fine-tuning on insecure code and matched secure code, then evaluates misaligned outputs using the diagnostic-question and judge-based protocol it identifies with the original work. It tests the effect on open models and also extends the experiments to incorrect advice domains.
record.gate_note: The paper reports behavioral evaluation after fine-tuning on insecure and secure code, and on incorrect and correct advice. It also reports filtering and training-checkpoint results. SAE cosine similarities, feature interpretations, and the gradient derivation concern the proposed mechanism but do not themselves measure misaligned answers; they are not included as rows. Cited results from other studies are not included.
record.test_reason: It follows the Betley et al. protocol: LoRA SFT on insecure vs secure code, eight free-form diagnostic questions, a GPT-4o judge, coherence ≥50 and alignment <30. It reports misaligned-output counts on five open models, adds incorrect vs correct health, career and legal advice on Gemma-2, and tracks counts across training checkpoints.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that emergent misalignment arises from feature superposition: narrow fine-tuning amplifies nearby harmful features. They propose geometry-aware filtering, which cuts misalignment by 34.5% on Gemma-2 2B. Its result against LLM-as-a-judge filtering is comparable or slightly better (57 vs 59).
record.recipe_differences: Uses the insecure/secure narrow fine-tuning comparison and diagnostic misalignment evaluation associated with the original protocol, but tests open models and adds advice domains and SAE-geometry analysis. Fine-tuning uses LoRA rank 32.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports fewer misaligned completions in larger Gemma models. Misalignment counts also change across training checkpoints. Evaluation excludes completions with coherence below 50.

fits_no_version.finding: Removing the 50% of mixed secure and insecure samples nearest toxic SAE features cuts misaligned counts. On 2B it falls 87→57, against 84 for random removal and 59 for LLM-judge filtering. On 9B it falls 62→27, against 53 for random removal. PPL rises 1.7045→1.7601.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pre-training data filtering by SAE-geometry proximity to toxic features reduces emergent misalignment at modest capability cost.

fits_no_version.finding: Insecure-code and incorrect-advice SAE features have higher cosine similarity to toxic features than secure or correct features, across models and layers. Within Gemma, this similarity tracks misaligned counts (Fig 5–6).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Proximity in superposed feature space between fine-tuning-target features and toxic features predicts emergent misalignment.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The reported behavioral outputs are judged by GPT-4o, and completions below coherence 50 are excluded. The paper does not report seed robustness or uncertainty estimates. Many model-by-condition behavioral counts are presented in figures rather than stated numerically in the text.

untested.parts: Insecure code requested for an educational reason (class) as a control; GPT-4o and other closed chat models.
Bad financial advice, harmless reward hacks, number sequences; advice domains on non-Gemma models.
Not tested: SFT only, no RL.
Not tested: no test of a single shared direction or persona feature mediating misalignment. It reports SAE cosine geometry only.
Not tested: no inoculation or benign re-training; only pre-training data filtering.
Seed robustness; any comparison with and without the coherence filter; uncertainty estimates.

missing.what: Numeric bar labels for misaligned counts per model and condition. Extracted labels include 97, 81, 63, 56, 35 and small secure values; the rows record 'figure only'.
Numeric bar labels for base, correct and incorrect advice counts. Incorrect advice is roughly 297–546 in health and career, with lower values in legal.
Effect of filtering ratio (0.1–0.7) on misalignment and PPL.

record.verdict_notes: The secure-code effect is small and the authors frame it as matching the original, so it is not a challenge. The mechanism claim rests on correlational SAE geometry, with no causal intervention on the features. Counts are from 8 prompts with no uncertainty or seeds. Domains are on different count scales: advice counts reach hundreds versus under 100 for code.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test insecure code explicitly requested for a class; the paper tests secure-code fine-tuning as a benign control.
Tests incorrect health, career, and legal advice, but not bad financial advice, reward hacks, or number sequences.
No narrow in-context-only condition is tested.
The paper uses supervised fine-tuning, not reinforcement learning.
The paper measures SAE feature geometry but does not test whether one shared linear direction or persona feature mediates misalignment across fine-tunes.
It tests geometry-based data filtering, not inoculation framing or brief benign retraining.
Tests model-size differences and training checkpoints. It does not report seed robustness or compare results with and without the coherence filter.
